texts.orig: Consider this book an instruction manual for recognizing chart patterns, discovering why they behave as they do, and learning what it means when you see one. texts.label: text
texts.orig: W hile working at Tandy Corporation, I hung on my offi ce  wall  a  price  chart  of  the  company's stock.  I  did  not  know  if  the  head-and-shoulders  top I  found was one or not, but it looked like a person's head in the middle of a pair of shoulders. To the left and right of that pattern, price dropped back to earth, making  it  seem  like  the  pattern  was  a  ghost  rising from a moat.

I  did  not  know  if  the  head-and-shoulders  top I  found was one or not, but it looked like a person's head in the middle of a pair of shoulders. To the left and right of that pattern, price dropped back to earth, making  it  seem  like  the  pattern  was  a  ghost  rising from a moat.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Th   at  was  my fi  rst  attempt  at  fi  nding  a  chart  pattern.  Since  that  time,  I  taught  myself  to  recognize chart patterns-a skill almost anyone can learn. Let us begin looking at a few charts to see how to recognize patterns.
texts.text: Th   at  was  my fi  rst  attempt  at  fi  nding  a  chart  pattern.  Since  that  time,  I  taught  myself  to  recognize chart patterns-a skill almost anyone can learn. Let us begin looking at a few charts to see how to recognize patterns.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Th   e empty chart is not empty at all, is it? Price bars form a mountain range that climbs higher until July after which a hiker walking on those bars would probably fall to their death. (See Exhibit 1.1.)
texts.text: Th   e empty chart is not empty at all, is it? Price bars form a mountain range that climbs higher until July after which a hiker walking on those bars would probably fall to their death. (See Exhibit 1.1.)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In  that  brief  description,  we  have  learned  two things:  Price  rises  until  July  and  then  dies.  If  you owned this stock, you would be looking for chart patterns that predict the coming decline. Why? Because you might want to sell before the tumble or act to protect your position.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In October, in addition to searching for the remains of our dead hiker, you would be looking for signs that the downward price trend had reversed. If it had, then you might want to buy the stock or buy more to capture the recovery.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: How do you fi  nd patterns that predict a decline? Begin with peaks.
texts.text: How do you fi  nd patterns that predict a decline? Begin with peaks.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When I look at a price chart, my eyes fi  nd peaks that stop at or near the same price. At line A, for example, several peaks approach or touch the upper red line. Th   at line represents overhead resistance .
texts.text: When I look at a price chart, my eyes fi  nd peaks that stop at or near the same price. At line A, for example, several peaks approach or touch the upper red line. Th   at line represents overhead resistance .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Overhead resistance, or just resistance, occurs when a stock stalls in an uptrend or reverses, creating a peak, often near the same price as it has in the past. Resistance is always above price.
texts.text: Overhead resistance, or just resistance, occurs when a stock stalls in an uptrend or reverses, creating a peak, often near the same price as it has in the past. Resistance is always above price.

The  two  lines  form  a  rectangle  chart  pattern.  The name of the chart pattern is not as important as how I found it. Just imagine a horizontal line that touches several peaks and another line that touches several valleys.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Underlying support, or just support, occurs when a falling stock stalls or reverses, creating a valley, often at the same price as it has in the past. Support is always below price.
texts.text: Underlying support, or just support, occurs when a falling stock stalls or reverses, creating a valley, often at the same price as it has in the past. Support is always below price.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Exhibit 1.3 highlights price valleys. In a manner similar to peaks, look for two or more valleys that bottom near  the  same  price.  Th ose  valleys  may  rest  upon  a fl   oor  where  support  is  strong  enough  to  launch  another move up. One example is CD.

texts.orig: Now that we have experimented with drawing trendlines, what are the guidelines and tips for their use? Here is a nine-item list.
texts.text: Now that we have experimented with drawing trendlines, what are the guidelines and tips for their use? Here is a nine-item list.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 1.  Trendlines  should  connect  at  least  two  peaks (minor highs) or two valleys (minor lows), preferably three or more.
texts.text: Trendlines  should  connect  at  least  two  peaks (minor highs) or two valleys (minor lows), preferably three or more.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 2.  Like  horseshoes  and  hand  grenades,  closeness counts. Price need not touch the trendline, but it should come close.
texts.text: Like  horseshoes  and  hand  grenades,  closeness counts. Price need not touch the trendline, but it should come close.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 3.  To  detect  a  trend  change,  draw  trendlines  along the valleys when price is trending up. Draw trendlines along the peaks in a declining stock.
texts.text: To  detect  a  trend  change,  draw  trendlines  along the valleys when price is trending up. Draw trendlines along the peaks in a declining stock.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Trendlines not only follow trends, but also outline chart patterns.
texts.text: Trendlines not only follow trends, but also outline chart patterns.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 4.	 Trendlines with widely spaced touches are more significant  than  are  those  with  narrow  ones  (I proved this).
texts.text: Trendlines with widely spaced touches are more significant  than  are  those  with  narrow  ones  (I proved this).

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 5.	 In 2006, I wrote in my book Getting Started in Chart Patterns ,  'Trendlines  are  like  diving  boards.  You get  a  bigger  bounce  from  a  longer  diving  board than a shorter one.'
texts.text: In 2006, I wrote in my book Getting Started in Chart Patterns ,  'Trendlines  are  like  diving  boards.  You get  a  bigger  bounce  from  a  longer  diving  board than a shorter one.'

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 6.	 Steep trendlines underperform shallow ones. That  means  larger  moves  occur  after  a  trendline pierce from a shallow trendline than a steep one.
texts.text: Steep trendlines underperform shallow ones. That  means  larger  moves  occur  after  a  trendline pierce from a shallow trendline than a steep one.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 7.	 Rising volume  along  an up-sloping trendline powers (a  larger  decline) price downward after a trendline break more than does a receding volume trend leading to the breakout.
texts.text: Rising volume  along  an up-sloping trendline powers (a  larger  decline) price downward after a trendline break more than does a receding volume trend leading to the breakout.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 8.	 For  downward  sloping  trendlines,  receding  volume leads to better performance after price pierces the trendline, moving up.
texts.text: For  downward  sloping  trendlines,  receding  volume leads to better performance after price pierces the trendline, moving up.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 9.	 Just  because  price  closes  above  a  down-sloping trendline or below an up-sloping one is no reason to believe that the trend has changed. It is only a hint of a trend change, not a guarantee.
texts.text: Just  because  price  closes  above  a  down-sloping trendline or below an up-sloping one is no reason to believe that the trend has changed. It is only a hint of a trend change, not a guarantee.

texts.label: text

If price breaks out in one direction, quickly reverses, and then trends, it busts the breakout. texts.text: B usted chart patterns' is a phrase I coined to help model the behavior of chart patterns when things go wrong. If price breaks out in one direction, quickly reverses, and then trends, it busts the breakout. Unfortunately, the busted ride can become a rollercoaster when a stock busts and busts again as it struggles to determine a trend direction. '

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Years ago, I was looking at chart patterns that failed to perform as expected when I noticed something unusual. Ascending triangles, for example, would break out downward and then reverse to begin a new trend that saw price soar like a glider in a thermal. 'I can make money from that,' I said.

table_cells.text: Occurs in areas of congestion (trendless markets) and close rapidly. Volume on the day of the gap can be high, but returns to normal in a day or two. No signifi cant highs (in uptrends) or lows (in downtrends) occur immediately after the gap. A distinctive curl as the gap closes is a key indication of this gap type.

Identifi es the start of a new trend and occurs on breakout from a consolidation region. Is accompanied by high volume on the day of the gap and continuing for several days. The trend continues long enough for several new highs (for uptrends) or new lows (downtrends) to occur after the gap.
Happens in the midst of a straight-line advance or decline. Price continues making new highs or lows without fi lling the gap. Volume is usually high, propelling price in the direction of the trend.

Occurs at the end of a trend on high volume. The gap is not followed by new minor highs or minor lows and the gap itself may be unusually tall. After the gap, price consolidates. Commonly occurs after a continuation gap. The gap closes quickly, usually within a week.

Price continues in the direction of the breakout for a few days, but then loops back to the breakout price.
After the stock returns to the breakout price, it leaves white space on the chart between the breakout and return.
The stock must return to the breakout price or trendline boundary within 30 days.

table_cells.text: The short-term price trend leading to a double bottom is down.
Look for two valleys that bottom near the same price. Near means within about 5 percent. The bottoms should look as if they are at the same price.
The time between bottoms varies, but two to seven weeks results in the best performance.
The peak between the two bottoms should measure at least 10 percent, but exceptions are numerous, making this guideline almost useless.
Volume is higher on the left bottom than the right, but this is an observation, not a requirement.
Price must close above the highest peak between the two bottoms. If price closes below the lowest bottom before confi rmation, it invalidates the double bottom.

Volume recedes, meaning it is higher on the left than the right, but each bottom can show signifi cant volume. Do not exclude a pattern because it has an unusual volume shape.
Price must confi rm the triple bottom by closing above the highest peak between the three bottoms.
